records.source: Μὴ πολλοὶ διδάσκαλοι γίνεσθε, ἀδελφοί μου, εἰδότες ὅτι μεῖζον κρίμα λημψόμεθα·
records.gloss: Not many teachers become, brothers of me, knowing that greater judgment we will receive;
pieces: Not many of you should become teachers, my {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, for you know that we who teach will be judged more strictly.

L.1: Not many [of you] should become teachers, my {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, knowing that we will receive a greater judgment.

R.1: My {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, not many of you should become teachers. You know that we teachers will be judged more strictly than others.

decisions.choice: teachers: those who taught the congregation, a recognized role
alternatives: anyone who gives advice or opinions
decisions.reason: Teachers had a named place in the early churches, next to prophets (Acts 13:1; 1 Corinthians 12:28). διδάσκαλοι here means that role. James is not telling believers to stop speaking about God, but warning against rushing to take a teaching role.

decisions.choice: we will receive: James counts himself among the teachers
decisions.reason: The verb changes from "you" to "we": λημψόμεθα. James is a teacher himself, and he puts himself under the same stricter judgment. The "we" of verse 2 ("we all stumble") then widens to everyone.

decisions.choice: a greater judgment: God judges teachers by a stricter standard
decisions.reason: κρίμα is the judgment God passes, and μεῖζον means greater or stricter. Those who teach others are answerable for their words (Matthew 12:36-37) and for what they have been given (Luke 12:48). Verse 2 gives the reason: everyone stumbles, and the teacher's tool is the tongue.

decisions.choice: my {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}
decisions.reason: Gender setting: James addresses the whole congregation, women and men.

decisions.choice: we who teach; we teachers
alternatives: we will receive a greater judgment
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable make the "we" explicit (m2) and say what a greater judgment means for the one judged.

records.heading: The power of the tongue

records.source: πολλὰ γὰρ πταίομεν ἅπαντες.
records.gloss: In many [ways] for stumble all.
pieces: For all of us stumble in many ways.

L.2: For we all stumble in many [ways].

R.2: All of us stumble and do wrong in many ways.

decisions.choice: stumble: fail, do wrong
decisions.reason: πταίω pictures tripping, and James uses it for failing to keep God's law: one who stumbles in one point is guilty of all (2:10). Here it means any wrongdoing, and verse 2 goes on to the wrongs done in speech.

decisions.choice: in many ways
decisions.reason: πολλὰ is used as an adverb. It can mean "in many respects" or "many times"; both say that no one escapes it. James includes himself in "we all".

decisions.choice: stumble and do wrong
decisions.reason: Readable keeps the picture and says what it means (m1).

records.source: εἴ τις ἐν λόγῳ οὐ πταίει, οὗτος τέλειος ἀνήρ, δυνατὸς χαλιναγωγῆσαι καὶ ὅλον τὸ σῶμα.
records.gloss: If anyone in word does not stumble, this one [is a] perfect man, able to bridle also the whole the body.
pieces: Anyone who does not stumble in what {{gender:they say|he says}} is a perfect {{gender:person|man}}, able to keep the whole body in check as well.

L.2: If anyone does not stumble in word, this one [is] a perfect {{gender:person|man}}, able to bridle the whole body as well.

R.2: Suppose someone never stumbles in what {{gender:they say|he says}}. That person is complete and mature. {{gender:They|He}} can also control {{gender:their|his}} whole body, the way a rider controls a horse with a bridle.

decisions.choice: in word: in what one says
decisions.reason: In 1:18-23 λόγος was the word of truth from God. Here, with "stumble", it is a person's own speech, the subject of the whole chapter (verses 5-12).

decisions.choice: perfect: complete, fully mature, not sinless
decisions.reason: τέλειος is the word of 1:4 ("perfect and complete, lacking nothing"). James has just said that everyone stumbles, so he does not mean anyone is free of all sin. He means a person whose speech is so governed that the rest of life is governed too.

decisions.choice: bridle: guide and restrain, as a rider does a horse
decisions.reason: χαλιναγωγῆσαι means to lead with a bridle. James used it in 1:26 for bridling the tongue, and verse 3 develops the picture: the small bit turns the whole horse. Whoever governs the tongue can govern the whole self.

decisions.choice: {{gender:person|man}}
decisions.reason: ἀνήρ usually means a man, but here it takes up "anyone" (τις) and speaks of any believer, so the gender setting applies. The pronouns for that person follow it.

decisions.choice: complete and mature; the way a rider controls a horse with a bridle
decisions.reason: Readable says what "perfect" means here (m2) and spells out the bridle picture, which verse 3 is about to use.

records.source: εἰ δὲ τῶν ἵππων τοὺς χαλινοὺς εἰς τὰ στόματα βάλλομεν εἰς τὸ πείθεσθαι αὐτοὺς ἡμῖν, καὶ ὅλον τὸ σῶμα αὐτῶν μετάγομεν.
records.gloss: If now of the horses the bits into the mouths we put for the to obey them us, also the whole the body of them we turn.
pieces: When we put bits into the mouths of horses to make them obey us, we steer their whole body as well.

L.3: Now if we put the bits into the mouths of horses so that they obey us, we also turn their whole body.

R.3: We put a small bit in the mouth of a horse to make it obey us. Then we can turn its whole body.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "now if"
alternatives: "look", calling attention, as at the start of verse 4
decisions.reason: Many manuscripts, including the text behind the King James Version, have a word meaning "look" here, which sounds almost the same as εἰ δὲ and matches ἰδοὺ in verse 4. The SBLGNT reads "now if". The picture and its point do not change. This note is written from general knowledge and must be checked against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: if: a plain fact used as a comparison
decisions.reason: James is not doubting that riders bridle horses. The "if" states something everyone knows, to compare it with the tongue (verse 5). The "whole body" picks up the end of verse 2.

decisions.choice: bits: the metal mouthpiece of a bridle
decisions.reason: χαλινός can mean the bridle as a whole, but put "into the mouths" it is the bit, the small piece the reins pull on. Its smallness is the point (verses 4-5).

decisions.choice: a small bit
decisions.reason: Readable adds "small" to make clear the point the comparison is making (verse 5).

records.source: ἰδοὺ καὶ τὰ πλοῖα, τηλικαῦτα ὄντα καὶ ὑπὸ ἀνέμων σκληρῶν ἐλαυνόμενα, μετάγεται ὑπὸ ἐλαχίστου πηδαλίου ὅπου ἡ ὁρμὴ τοῦ εὐθύνοντος βούλεται·
records.gloss: Look also the ships, so great being and by winds hard being driven, are turned by a very small rudder wherever the impulse of the [one] steering wants;
pieces: Or look at ships. They are so large, and fierce winds drive them, yet a very small rudder turns them wherever the pilot means to go.

L.4: Look also at the ships: though they are so large and are driven by hard winds, they are turned by a very small rudder wherever the impulse of the one steering wishes.

R.4: Or think about ships. They are very big, and strong winds push them along. But a very small rudder turns them wherever the pilot wants to go.

decisions.choice: look: a call to notice the example
decisions.reason: ἰδοὺ calls for attention to a new picture. James uses it again in verse 5 and in chapter 5 (5:4, 5:7, 5:9, 5:11).

decisions.choice: though they are so large and driven by strong winds
decisions.reason: The two participles ὄντα and ἐλαυνόμενα describe the ships in a way that sets up a contrast: large and driven by strong forces, and yet steered by a tiny thing.

decisions.choice: the impulse of the one steering: the pilot's will, where he means to go
alternatives: the push of the pilot's hand on the tiller
decisions.reason: ὁρμὴ means a strong urge or intention. The point is that the will of one person directs the whole ship through the small rudder, as the tongue directs a life.

decisions.choice: wherever the pilot means to go; wherever the pilot wants to go
alternatives: wherever the impulse of the one steering wishes
decisions.reason: The participle εὐθύνοντος is "the one steering", the pilot. Balanced and Readable name him and turn "impulse" into what he means or wants.

records.source: οὕτως καὶ ἡ γλῶσσα μικρὸν μέλος ἐστὶν καὶ μεγάλα αὐχεῖ.
records.gloss: So also the tongue a small member is and great things boasts.
pieces: In the same way the tongue is a small part of the body, yet it boasts of great things.

L.5: So also the tongue is a small member, and it boasts great things.

R.5: The tongue is like that. It is a small part of the body, but it brags about big things.

decisions.choice: member: a part of the body
decisions.reason: μέλος is a limb or organ. James speaks of the body and its members again in verse 6 and in 4:1.

decisions.choice: boasts great things: makes great claims, and has great power to match
decisions.reason: αὐχεῖ is to boast. Set beside the bit and the rudder, it means that this small part speaks big and sets big things in motion, for good or harm. The next sentence turns to the harm.

decisions.choice: a small part of the body
decisions.reason: "Member" no longer means a part of the body for most readers.

records.source: Ἰδοὺ ἡλίκον πῦρ ἡλίκην ὕλην ἀνάπτει·
records.gloss: Look how small a fire how great a forest sets ablaze;
pieces: Look how small a flame can set so large a forest on fire!

L.5: Look how small a fire sets ablaze how great a forest!

R.5: Just think about it. A tiny flame can set a whole big forest on fire.

decisions.choice: how small ... how great: the same word in both senses
decisions.reason: ἡλίκος asks "how large?" and can point either way. James uses it twice, first for the small fire and then for the great forest, so the one word carries the contrast.

decisions.choice: forest: woodland or dry brush
decisions.reason: ὕλην can be timber, firewood or woodland. With "how great" it is a large stretch of wood or brush, the kind of land a summer fire could sweep through.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "how small a fire"
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts, including the text behind the King James Version, have a plain word for "little" in place of the first "how small". The meaning is the same; the SBLGNT reading keeps the play on one word (m1). This note is written from general knowledge and must be checked against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: flame
decisions.reason: "Flame" says plainly that the fire is small at the start; "fire" returns in verse 6.

records.source: καὶ ἡ γλῶσσα πῦρ, ὁ κόσμος τῆς ἀδικίας ἡ γλῶσσα καθίσταται ἐν τοῖς μέλεσιν ἡμῶν, ἡ σπιλοῦσα ὅλον τὸ σῶμα καὶ φλογίζουσα τὸν τροχὸν τῆς γενέσεως καὶ φλογιζομένη ὑπὸ τῆς γεέννης.
records.gloss: And the tongue [is a] fire, the world of the unrighteousness the tongue is set among the members of us, the [one] staining whole the body and setting on fire the wheel of the existence and being set on fire by the Gehenna.
pieces: And the tongue is a fire. It takes its place among the parts of our body as a world of wrongdoing: it stains the whole body, it sets the whole course of life on fire, and it is itself set on fire by hell.

L.6: And the tongue [is] a fire. As the world of unrighteousness, the tongue is set among our members, staining the whole body and setting on fire the wheel of existence, and being set on fire by Gehenna.

R.6: The tongue is a fire too. It is a whole world of evil, there among the parts of our body. It stains the whole body. It sets the whole of life on fire, and its fire comes from hell.

decisions.choice: the tongue is set among our members as the world of unrighteousness
alternatives: the tongue is a fire, a world of unrighteousness; the tongue is set among our members, staining ...
decisions.reason: The sentence is hard to divide. The SBLGNT puts a comma after πῦρ ("fire") and none after ἀδικίας, which makes "the world of unrighteousness" go with καθίσταται: among the parts of the body, the tongue stands as that world. Others join "world of unrighteousness" to "fire" and start a new clause at the second "the tongue". The meaning is close either way.

decisions.choice: world: a whole realm, the sum of all wrongdoing in small
alternatives: an ornament (an old sense of the word)
decisions.reason: κόσμος usually means the world. Here "the world of unrighteousness" is the whole range of wrongdoing gathered into one small part of the body. It looks ahead to 4:4, where friendship with the world is enmity with God.

decisions.choice: the wheel of existence: the whole course of human life, from birth on
alternatives: the cycle of birth and death taught by some Greek religions
the course of the natural world
decisions.reason: τροχὸν is a wheel and γενέσεως is birth or existence (the same word as "natural face" in 1:23). The phrase was used in Greek writing for the round of life. James borrows it to say that the tongue can set a whole life burning, from beginning to end, not to teach anything about rebirth.

decisions.choice: Gehenna: the place of final judgment, and the power of evil behind it
decisions.reason: Gehenna was the Valley of Hinnom south of Jerusalem, where children had been burned in sacrifice (2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 7:31-32). Its name came to mean the place of final punishment, as in Jesus' words (Matthew 5:22; Mark 9:43). This is its only use outside the Gospels. The tongue's fire is lit from there: its destructive power comes from evil itself.

decisions.choice: Gehenna (Literal); hell (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the place name so the reader can see what James wrote; Balanced and Readable use the English word for what the name stands for (m4).

decisions.choice: unrighteousness (Literal); wrongdoing (Balanced); evil (Readable)
decisions.reason: ἀδικίας is the opposite of righteousness. Literal keeps the form; Balanced and Readable use plainer words for doing wrong.

records.source: πᾶσα γὰρ φύσις θηρίων τε καὶ πετεινῶν ἑρπετῶν τε καὶ ἐναλίων δαμάζεται καὶ δεδάμασται τῇ φύσει τῇ ἀνθρωπίνῃ·
records.gloss: Every for kind of beasts both and birds, of reptiles both and sea creatures, is tamed and has been tamed by the nature the human;
pieces: Every kind of wild animal and bird, of reptile and creature of the sea, is being tamed and has been tamed by humankind.

L.7: For every kind of wild animals and birds, of reptiles and sea creatures, is being tamed and has been tamed by the human kind.

R.7: People can tame every kind of animal: wild animals, birds, reptiles and sea creatures. People have tamed them all.

decisions.choice: four kinds of creatures: an echo of Genesis
decisions.reason: Wild animals, birds, creeping things and creatures of the sea are the groups over which God gave humans rule (Genesis 1:26; 9:2; compare Psalm 8:8-9). Humans have done what they were made to do with every creature, but not with their own tongue (verse 8).

decisions.choice: kind ... human kind: the same word for animal and human nature
decisions.reason: φύσις is used twice: every "kind" of creature is tamed by the human "kind". The repetition sets humanity over against all other creatures.

decisions.choice: is being tamed and has been tamed: an ongoing work, and a done one
decisions.reason: The present δαμάζεται says it goes on; the perfect δεδάμασται says it has been achieved. Both make the contrast in verse 8 sharper.

decisions.choice: People can tame ...; People have tamed them all.
alternatives: Every kind ... is being tamed and has been tamed by humankind
decisions.reason: Readable makes "people" the subject and gives the two verbs a sentence each.

records.source: τὴν δὲ γλῶσσαν οὐδεὶς δαμάσαι δύναται ἀνθρώπων· ἀκατάστατον κακόν, μεστὴ ἰοῦ θανατηφόρου.
records.gloss: But the tongue no one to tame is able of men; a restless evil, full of poison deadly.
pieces: But no human being can tame the tongue. It is a restless evil, full of deadly poison.

L.8: But no one of {{gender:people|men}} is able to tame the tongue: a restless evil, full of deadly poison.

R.8: But no one can tame the tongue. It is evil, and it never rests. It is full of poison that kills.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "restless"
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts, including the text behind the King James Version, have a similar word meaning "that cannot be restrained". The SBLGNT reads ἀκατάστατον, "restless, unstable". The sense is close. This note is written from general knowledge and must be checked against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: restless: unstable, never at rest
decisions.reason: ἀκατάστατος is the word for the double-minded man in 1:8, and its noun returns in verse 16 ("disorder"). The tongue is like a wild animal that cannot be kept still.

decisions.choice: full of deadly poison: the poison of the serpent
decisions.reason: The psalm says of the wicked, "the poison of vipers is under their lips" (Psalm 140:4), and Paul quotes it of human speech (Romans 3:13). Like a snake, the tongue can kill.

decisions.choice: no one of people: no human being, by human power
alternatives: no one at all can, not even God
decisions.reason: ἀνθρώπων sets the tongue against verse 7: humans tame every creature but not this. James does not say God cannot; his call to receive wisdom from God (1:5; 3:17) assumes help comes from above.

records.source: ἐν αὐτῇ εὐλογοῦμεν τὸν κύριον καὶ πατέρα, καὶ ἐν αὐτῇ καταρώμεθα τοὺς ἀνθρώπους τοὺς καθ’ ὁμοίωσιν θεοῦ γεγονότας·
records.gloss: With it we bless the Lord and Father, and with it we curse the men the [ones] according to likeness of God having been made;
pieces: With the tongue we bless the Lord and Father, and with it we curse human beings, who have been made in the likeness of God.

L.9: With it we bless the Lord and Father, and with it we curse {{gender:people|men}}, who have been made according to the likeness of God.

R.9: We use our tongues to praise God, our Lord and Father. Then we use them to curse people, and God made those people to be like {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "the Lord and Father"
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts, including the text behind the King James Version, read "God" in place of "Lord". The SBLGNT reading "the Lord and Father" is found only here in the New Testament. The one meant is the same. This note is written from general knowledge and must be checked against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: the Lord and Father: God, named with one article as both
alternatives: the Lord Jesus and the Father
decisions.reason: One article governs both words, so they name one person: God, who is Lord and Father (compare "God and Father" in 1:27).

decisions.choice: made according to the likeness of God: Genesis 1:26
decisions.reason: ὁμοίωσιν is the word of Genesis 1:26 in the Greek Old Testament: "let us make humankind ... according to our likeness". The perfect γεγονότας says people still bear that likeness. To curse a person is to curse what bears God's likeness, so blessing God and cursing people with one tongue cannot fit together (Genesis 9:6).

decisions.choice: bless and curse: words spoken to God and against people
decisions.reason: To bless God is to praise him; Jewish prayers began "Blessed be God" (as Luke 1:68; 2 Corinthians 1:3). To curse a person was to call down harm on them. Both are acts of speech, the tongue's best and worst.

decisions.choice: praise God, our Lord and Father
decisions.reason: Readable says "praise" for blessing God (m4) and names God, so a young reader knows who is meant (m2).

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}
decisions.reason: Readable turns "the likeness of God" into "to be like him"; the pronoun is for God.

records.source: ἐκ τοῦ αὐτοῦ στόματος ἐξέρχεται εὐλογία καὶ κατάρα.
records.gloss: From the same mouth comes out blessing and cursing.
pieces: Blessing and cursing come out of the same mouth.

L.10: From the same mouth come out blessing and cursing.

R.10: Praise and curses come out of the same mouth.

decisions.choice: blessing and cursing: words that call for good and for harm
decisions.reason: The nouns pick up the verbs of verse 9. "The same mouth" is the point: one source gives out opposites, which verses 11-12 show is against nature.

decisions.choice: praise
decisions.reason: As in verse 9, Readable uses "praise" for the blessing of God.

records.source: οὐ χρή, ἀδελφοί μου, ταῦτα οὕτως γίνεσθαι.
records.gloss: Not it is fitting, brothers of me, these things so to happen.
pieces: My {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, it must not be this way.

L.10: [It is] not fitting, my {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, [for] these things to be so.

R.10: My {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, this is wrong. It should not happen.

decisions.choice: it is not fitting: it ought not to be
decisions.reason: χρή, found only here in the New Testament, says what ought to be. James does not argue further; he simply calls it wrong, and then shows from nature how out of place it is.

decisions.choice: my {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}
decisions.reason: Gender setting: James addresses the whole congregation, women and men.

records.source: μήτι ἡ πηγὴ ἐκ τῆς αὐτῆς ὀπῆς βρύει τὸ γλυκὺ καὶ τὸ πικρόν;
records.gloss: Surely not the spring from the same opening pours out the sweet and the bitter?
pieces: Does a spring pour out fresh water and bitter water from the same opening?

L.11: A spring does not pour out from the same opening the sweet and the bitter, does it?

R.11: Fresh water and bitter water do not flow out of the same spring, do they?

decisions.choice: a question that expects the answer no
decisions.reason: μήτι marks a question expecting "no". Literal shows this with "does it?"; the Balanced question is plain enough to be heard the same way.

decisions.choice: sweet and bitter: water good to drink, and water that is not
decisions.reason: "Sweet" water is fresh water; "bitter" water is brackish or full of minerals, as at Marah (Exodus 15:23). The same word "bitter" returns for "bitter jealousy" in verse 14.

decisions.choice: fresh water and bitter water
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable supply "water", which the Greek leaves understood.

records.source: μὴ δύναται, ἀδελφοί μου, συκῆ ἐλαίας ποιῆσαι ἢ ἄμπελος σῦκα;
records.gloss: Not is able, brothers of me, a fig tree olives to produce or a vine figs?
pieces: My {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, can a fig tree yield olives, or a grapevine yield figs?

L.12: A fig tree is not able, my {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, to produce olives, or a vine figs, is it?

R.12: My {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, a fig tree cannot grow olives, and a grapevine cannot grow figs.

decisions.choice: a question that expects the answer no
decisions.reason: μὴ again expects "no". Each plant bears its own kind of fruit.

decisions.choice: the plant and its fruit: Jesus' teaching on trees and fruit
decisions.reason: Jesus asked whether figs are gathered from thistles, and said a tree is known by its fruit (Matthew 7:16-20; Luke 6:43-44). James uses the same kind of picture for speech: what comes out shows what is inside (compare verse 17, "good fruits").

decisions.choice: my {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}
decisions.reason: Gender setting: James addresses the whole congregation, women and men.

decisions.choice: a statement: a fig tree cannot grow olives
alternatives: a question: can a fig tree yield olives?
decisions.reason: Readable gives the expected answer as a plain statement (m1).

records.source: οὔτε ἁλυκὸν γλυκὺ ποιῆσαι ὕδωρ.
records.gloss: Nor salt sweet to produce water.
pieces: Nor can a salt spring give fresh water.

R.12: And a salty spring cannot give fresh water.

decisions.choice: follow SBLGNT: "nor can salt produce sweet water"
alternatives: "so no spring yields both salt water and fresh"
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts, including the text behind the King James Version, have a longer sentence that brings back the spring of verse 11. The SBLGNT has the short form. The point is the same. This note is written from general knowledge and must be checked against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: salt [water] is the subject; "can" carries over from the question before
alternatives: "nor can [a spring] make salt water sweet"
decisions.reason: ἁλυκὸν is a neuter adjective standing alone as the subject, "a salt [source]", and ποιῆσαι depends on "is able" in the first half of the verse. A salt spring cannot give fresh water, any more than a fig tree can give olives.

decisions.choice: a salt spring; a salty spring
decisions.reason: The spring is understood from verse 11; Balanced and Readable supply it.

records.source: Τίς σοφὸς καὶ ἐπιστήμων ἐν ὑμῖν;
records.gloss: Who [is] wise and understanding among you?
pieces: Who among you is wise and understanding?

L.13: Who [is] wise and understanding among you?

R.13: Who among you is wise and understands things well?

decisions.choice: wise and understanding: the qualities of those chosen to lead
decisions.reason: σοφὸς and ἐπιστήμων stand together in the Greek Old Testament for the leaders Moses was to appoint (Deuteronomy 1:13) and for Israel itself when it keeps God's law (Deuteronomy 4:6). The question looks back to verse 1: those who want to teach must show this wisdom.

decisions.choice: a real question, used as a challenge
decisions.reason: The question invites anyone who thinks of themselves as wise to step forward, and the next sentence tells them how to prove it.

records.heading: The wisdom from above

records.source: δειξάτω ἐκ τῆς καλῆς ἀναστροφῆς τὰ ἔργα αὐτοῦ ἐν πραΰτητι σοφίας.
records.gloss: Let him show from the good conduct the works of him in gentleness of wisdom.
pieces: Let {{gender:them|him}} show it by a good life, by works done in the gentleness that wisdom gives.

L.13: Let {{gender:them|him}} show by the good way of life {{gender:their|his}} works in [the] gentleness of wisdom.

R.13: Then {{gender:they|he}} should show it by living a good life. {{gender:Their|His}} actions should be done with the gentleness that comes from wisdom.

decisions.choice: good conduct: a way of life
decisions.reason: ἀναστροφῆς is the whole way a person lives, seen by others. Wisdom is shown, not claimed, as faith is shown by works (2:18).

decisions.choice: gentleness: strength held in check, not weakness
decisions.reason: πραΰτης is the gentle spirit of one who does not push for their own way (Matthew 5:5; 11:29). James asked for it in receiving the word (1:21); here it marks true wisdom, against the jealousy and ambition of verse 14.

decisions.choice: the gentleness of wisdom: gentleness that wisdom produces
decisions.reason: The genitive σοφίας says where the gentleness comes from: true wisdom makes a person gentle.

decisions.choice: {{gender:them|him}}, {{gender:their|his}}
decisions.reason: Gender setting: the imperative "let [that one] show" and αὐτοῦ refer to anyone among them who is wise.

decisions.choice: actions
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced keep "works", the word of 2:14-26. Readable says "actions", the plain word for what someone does.

records.source: εἰ δὲ ζῆλον πικρὸν ἔχετε καὶ ἐριθείαν ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ ὑμῶν, μὴ κατακαυχᾶσθε καὶ ψεύδεσθε κατὰ τῆς ἀληθείας.
records.gloss: But if jealousy bitter you have and selfish ambition in the heart of you, do not boast and lie against the truth.
pieces: But if bitter jealousy and selfish ambition fill your hearts, do not boast, and do not lie against the truth.

L.14: But if you have bitter jealousy and selfish ambition in your heart, do not boast and lie against the truth.

R.14: But maybe your heart is full of bitter jealousy, and you only want to get ahead of others. Then do not brag about how wise you are, and do not lie against the truth.

decisions.choice: bitter jealousy: resentful rivalry
alternatives: zeal, eager devotion (a good sense of the same word)
decisions.reason: ζῆλος can be good zeal, but with "bitter" it is the jealous rivalry that resents others. "Bitter" recalls the bitter water of verse 11.

decisions.choice: selfish ambition: seeking one's own advantage, forming factions
decisions.reason: ἐριθεία was a word for working for one's own gain, and came to mean self-seeking rivalry (Philippians 2:3; Galatians 5:20). It returns in verse 16.

decisions.choice: boasting and lying are one act: claiming wisdom while the heart is full of rivalry
alternatives: two separate commands about two different sins
decisions.reason: κατακαυχᾶσθε means to boast, even to boast over others. A person who claims to be wise while acting from jealousy denies the truth by that very claim. Verse 15 says such "wisdom" is not from above.

decisions.choice: fill your hearts
decisions.reason: Balanced says the heart is filled with these things; "hearts" is plural because "you" is plural.

decisions.choice: you only want to get ahead of others; brag about how wise you are
decisions.reason: Readable explains "selfish ambition" and says what the boasting is about, from verse 13 (m3).

records.source: οὐκ ἔστιν αὕτη ἡ σοφία ἄνωθεν κατερχομένη, ἀλλὰ ἐπίγειος, ψυχική, δαιμονιώδης·
records.gloss: Not is this the wisdom from above coming down, but earthly, natural, demonic;
pieces: This is not the kind of wisdom that comes down from above; it belongs to the earth, to mere human nature, and to demons.

L.15: This wisdom is not coming down from above, but [is] earthly, natural, demonic.

R.15: That kind of wisdom does not come down from God above. It comes from this world. It comes from people who do not have God's Spirit, and it comes from demons.

decisions.choice: from above: from God
decisions.reason: ἄνωθεν points to God, the giver of every good and perfect gift, which comes down "from above" (1:17), and who gives wisdom to all who ask (1:5).

decisions.choice: natural: belonging to human life without God's Spirit
decisions.reason: ψυχική comes from the word for soul or life. Paul uses it for the person without the Spirit (1 Corinthians 2:14), and Jude for those "not having the Spirit" (Jude 19). It is not "spiritual" in the sense James means.

decisions.choice: demonic: like the demons, and from them
decisions.reason: δαιμονιώδης is found only here in the New Testament. Such wisdom is the kind demons have: they too "believe" (2:19) without being changed. The three words move downward from earth to self to demons.

decisions.choice: from God above; from this world; from people who do not have God's Spirit
decisions.reason: Readable says who is "above" (m1) and explains the two adjectives as sources.

records.source: ὅπου γὰρ ζῆλος καὶ ἐριθεία, ἐκεῖ ἀκαταστασία καὶ πᾶν φαῦλον πρᾶγμα.
records.gloss: Where for jealousy and selfish ambition, there disorder and every bad deed.
pieces: Wherever jealousy and selfish ambition are found, disorder follows, and every kind of evil deed.

L.16: For where jealousy and selfish ambition [are], there [is] disorder and every evil deed.

R.16: When people are jealous and selfish, things fall apart, and all kinds of evil things happen.

decisions.choice: disorder: unrest, confusion that breaks up a community
decisions.reason: ἀκαταστασία is used for social upheaval (Luke 21:9) and for confusion in a church gathering, the opposite of peace (1 Corinthians 14:33). It belongs with "restless" in verse 8 and "unstable" in 1:8.

decisions.choice: evil: worthless and bad
decisions.reason: φαῦλον is what is base or worthless, and so wicked (John 3:20; 5:29). "Every" says there is no limit to what follows.

decisions.choice: follows
decisions.reason: Balanced turns "there [is]" into "follows", which says the same link of cause and result.

decisions.choice: things fall apart
decisions.reason: Readable puts "disorder" into everyday words.

records.source: ἡ δὲ ἄνωθεν σοφία πρῶτον μὲν ἁγνή ἐστιν, ἔπειτα εἰρηνική, ἐπιεικής, εὐπειθής, μεστὴ ἐλέους καὶ καρπῶν ἀγαθῶν, ἀδιάκριτος, ἀνυπόκριτος·
records.gloss: But the from above wisdom first indeed pure is, then peaceable, gentle, open to persuasion, full of mercy and fruits good, impartial, without hypocrisy;
pieces: But the wisdom from above is, first of all, pure. It also makes for peace; it is gentle and willing to yield; it is full of mercy and of good fruits; it plays no favorites, and it is free of pretense.

L.17: But the wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, ready to yield, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, without hypocrisy.

R.17: But the wisdom from above is pure, first of all. It also loves peace. It is gentle, and it is willing to listen to others. It is full of mercy, and it does many good things. It treats everyone fairly, and it is honest, not fake.

decisions.choice: first pure: purity comes first and the rest flows from it
alternatives: the first in a list of equals
decisions.reason: "First ... then" (πρῶτον ... ἔπειτα) sets purity apart. ἁγνή is moral purity, a heart free of the mixed motives of verse 14 (compare 4:8, "purify your hearts").

decisions.choice: ready to yield: open to persuasion, easy to reason with
decisions.reason: εὐπειθής, found only here in the New Testament, describes one who can be persuaded and does not dig in. It is the opposite of the stubborn self-seeking of verse 14.

decisions.choice: without partiality
alternatives: without wavering or doubt (as the related verb in 1:6)
decisions.reason: ἀδιάκριτος is built on the verb used for doubting in 1:6 and for making distinctions between people in 2:4. It may mean "undivided, not wavering" or "not taking sides". The list is about how wisdom treats others, and James has warned against favoritism (2:1-4), so "without partiality" is preferred.

decisions.choice: good fruits: good deeds
decisions.reason: Fruit is what a life produces (verse 12; Matthew 7:16-20). Wisdom shows itself in mercy and good actions, as faith does in works (2:14-26).

decisions.choice: makes for peace; loves peace; free of pretense; honest, not fake
decisions.reason: εἰρηνική is the adjective from "peace", not the noun itself, so the levels may phrase it. ἀνυπόκριτος means without play-acting; Balanced and Readable say it plainly.

decisions.choice: willing to listen to others; does many good things
alternatives: ready to yield; full of good fruits
decisions.reason: Readable explains the two less familiar phrases (m2, m4).

records.source: καρπὸς δὲ δικαιοσύνης ἐν εἰρήνῃ σπείρεται τοῖς ποιοῦσιν εἰρήνην.
records.gloss: Fruit and of righteousness in peace is sown by/for the [ones] making peace.
pieces: Those who make peace sow their seed in peace, and the fruit it yields is righteousness.

L.18: And [the] fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.

R.18: People who make peace plant their seeds in peace, and what grows from them is righteousness.

decisions.choice: fruit of righteousness: the fruit that is righteousness
decisions.reason: The genitive δικαιοσύνης can name the fruit itself or its source. Read as "the fruit which is righteousness", the harvest of a peaceable life is right living before God and others (compare Philippians 1:11; Hebrews 12:11).

decisions.choice: by those who make peace
alternatives: for those who make peace, who receive the harvest
decisions.reason: The dative ποιοῦσιν can name who does the sowing or who benefits from it. With "sown", it most naturally names the sowers; but the harvest also belongs to them, so either reading leaves peacemakers reaping righteousness.

decisions.choice: making peace: Jesus' blessing on peacemakers
decisions.reason: Jesus said, "Blessed are the peacemakers" (Matthew 5:9), and Isaiah tied righteousness and peace together (Isaiah 32:17). The verse closes the section by setting peace against the disorder of verse 16.

decisions.choice: the peacemakers are the subject: they sow, and righteousness is what grows
alternatives: the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable make the sowers the subject so the passive sentence reads naturally; the picture of seed and fruit is kept (m1, m2).
